label: Inference on Parameters
notes: This chapter turns the matrix Langevin and Bingham distributions on the Stiefel manifold into an inference problem. We observe a sample of orientation matrices and ask which modal orientation and which concentration parameter generated them. Maximum likelihood, sufficiency, and hypothesis testing organize every result that follows here.

label: Sampling on the Stiefel Manifold
notes: A point of the Stiefel manifold is a matrix with orthonormal columns, an orientation frame rather than a free vector. Each observation is one such frame, so the sample is a cloud of frames scattered around an unknown modal frame whose recovery is the central estimation task of this chapter.

label: The Matrix Langevin Model
notes: The matrix Langevin density is proportional to the exponential of the trace of F transpose X. The parameter matrix F factors into a modal orientation and a concentration, so its singular value decomposition cleanly separates where the mode points from how tightly the sample concentrates around it.

label: The Sample Mean Matrix
notes: Averaging the observed frames entrywise gives the sample mean matrix, the resultant of the data. Because the density depends on the data only through the trace against F, this average is a sufficient statistic. All the information the sample carries about the parameter is compressed into this one matrix.

label: The Likelihood Equations
notes: Writing the log likelihood for the Langevin model and differentiating in the parameter matrix produces the score equations. Setting the score to zero shows the maximum likelihood estimate must match the observed mean matrix to the expected value predicted by the normalizing constant, a balance condition we solve next.

label: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
notes: The estimator balances two forces. The observed resultant pulls the parameter toward the data, while the derivative of the log normalizing constant pulls back toward dispersion. The maximum likelihood estimate sits where these tensions cancel, mirroring how exponential family means equate observed and expected sufficient statistics.

label: Estimating the Modal Orientation
notes: Decompose the sample mean matrix by singular value decomposition. The left and right orthogonal factors estimate the modal orientation directly, while the singular values feed the concentration estimate. The modal frame is therefore read off the polar part of the resultant, a clean separation of direction from strength.

label: Estimating the Concentration
notes: With the orientation fixed, the concentration parameters solve a one dimensional equation per singular value. The ratio of a derivative of the normalizing constant to itself must equal the observed singular value. Larger singular values force larger concentrations, so a tightly clustered sample yields a sharply peaked fitted model.

label: The Matrix Bingham Model
notes: The Bingham density replaces the linear trace with a quadratic form, the trace of X transpose A X. It is antipodally symmetric, so it models axes rather than directions. Inference targets the symmetric parameter matrix A, whose eigenvectors give modal axes and whose eigenvalues give concentrations.

label: Testing Uniformity
notes: The uniform distribution is the null model of no preferred orientation, the Langevin density with parameter matrix zero. Testing uniformity asks whether the observed resultant is large enough to reject pure randomness. The mean matrix near zero supports uniformity, while a strong resultant is evidence against it.

label: Testing a Specified Orientation
notes: To test a claimed modal orientation we compare the fitted estimate against the hypothesized frame. The likelihood ratio contrasts the maximized likelihood with the likelihood constrained to the specified orientation. Under the null its statistic has a known limiting chi squared law, giving calibrated rejection regions.

label: Recap and Workflow
notes: The inference pipeline is compact. Form the sample mean matrix, take its singular value decomposition, read off the modal orientation, solve for the concentration, then test uniformity or a specified orientation. Sufficiency guarantees nothing is lost, and the score balance gives every estimate a clear interpretation.
